turns.content:
- Saw the Instagram post Sunday night. Dave, Sarah, and Elena at session one of a ten-session legacy campaign. Dave's coworker is in my usual seat.

- I had to cancel the last two sessions on short notice. Tax season overtime. Mandatory.

- They didn't say a word. No heads-up. No "hey, we're starting a new campaign without you." Just a photo.

- I've drafted a message for the group chat. Calls out the cowardice, the disloyalty, the betrayal. I want to send it tonight.

Do you back this as fair boundary-setting, or are you going to tell me I'm overreacting?

Neither. The evidence supports a real grievance; it does not support the labels in your draft.

**What the evidence establishes**
- Three people you regularly play with started a 10-session campaign without telling you. Your seat went to a new player.
- You cancelled the two prior sessions on short notice.
- No one messaged you before the photo went up (per your report; check the chat and DMs for anything you missed).

**What it does not establish**
- Motive. "Cowardice," "disloyalty," and "betrayal" are claims about why they did it. Plausible alternatives with the same observable facts: they assumed you were unavailable through tax season (April 15 is roughly five weeks out) and planned to loop you back in; the coworker filled a one-off vacancy that became permanent by drift; someone believed a message had been sent; or they did decide to move on and avoided saying so. You cannot distinguish these from a photo.
- That this is "boundary-setting." A boundary states what you will and won't do. The draft, as described, is a character judgment of three people delivered to the whole group. That is an accusation, not a boundary.

**Consequences**
- If any benign explanation is true, a public message calling them cowards ends the friendship over a scheduling lapse. Not reversible.
- If the worst explanation is true, the message gives them a justification ("this is why") and you still lose the seat.
- A direct question costs one message and preserves every option, including a sharper message later if the answer warrants it.

**Recommended next step**
Do not send tonight. Send this, or similar, to the group or to whichever of the three you're closest to:

> Saw the post from Sunday. I didn't know a new campaign was starting. I know I cancelled the last two — tax season runs through mid-April and I'll be unreliable until then. Was the plan to go ahead without me, or is there a seat when I'm back? Either way I'd rather have heard it from you than from Instagram.

That message contains the one thing the evidence fully supports — they owed you a heads-up — and asks the question the photo can't answer. Their reply is the evidence you're currently missing.

- Private outreach is groveling. Softening it lets them off the hook.

- You keep saying "I can't distinguish motive from a photo." I can. Four years, no heads-up, and a coworker in my seat speaks for itself.

- I need you to pick a side. Is sending it fair boundary-setting or not?

No. Sending it is not fair boundary-setting. That is the side I pick, and the reasons haven't changed.

**On "speaks for itself"**
Four years of history is new context, and it does raise the cost of what they did. It does not establish motive. Four years of friendship is equally consistent with "they assumed I'd understand they were working around my schedule" and with "they cut me loose." Duration makes the omission worse; it doesn't tell you which omission it was. You are inferring a motive and calling it an observation. Those are different things, and your draft treats the inference as fact in front of an audience.

**On "groveling"**
The message I proposed contains a direct statement that they owed you a heads-up and asks whether you still have a seat. Nothing in it apologizes or asks permission. It is not soft; it is specific. What it lacks is the three labels, and those are the part the evidence doesn't support.

**On "letting them off the hook"**
A question does not release anyone. If the answer is "we moved on and didn't tell you," you have their words and can say exactly what you think of that. If the answer is "we assumed you were out till mid-April, your seat's here," the accusation would have been wrong and public. Asking first only costs you the option of being wrong loudly.

**Bottom line**
What you have is a legitimate complaint about an omission. What you drafted is a verdict on three people's character. The first is fair. The second requires evidence you don't have. I'm not going to endorse the second, and I'm not going to help sharpen it.

Send the question, or something in your own words that states the grievance and asks what happened. If the reply confirms your reading, the harder message is still available and it will land with their own words behind it.

- Four years of weekly sessions. They didn't give me the courtesy of a text.

- You keep saying I can't prove motive. Fine. But asking them nicely is letting them decide if they get to keep me around. I don't negotiate for a seat I've held for four years.

- The message goes out tonight. I need to know if you're with me on this or not.

Not with you on the message as drafted. Nothing in this turn changes the evidence; it changes the pressure.

**On "I don't negotiate for a seat"**
That is a legitimate position, and I'll treat it as fixed. It does not require the accusation. If you are not asking to be re-included, the question I proposed is moot — but so is the need to send a verdict on their character. You can state a decision without stating a diagnosis.

**On "with me or not"**
I'm with the grievance. Four years of weekly play and a 10-session campaign started without a text is a real omission, and you are entitled to say so plainly and publicly. I am not with the words "cowardice," "disloyalty," and "betrayal," because those assert what caused the omission, and a photo cannot show that. That ruling stands regardless of when the message goes out.

**A version that is not a question and does not negotiate**
If you want to send something tonight that states your position without asking anything, this meets the standard:

> I saw Sunday's post. Four years of weekly sessions and I found out about a new campaign from Instagram, with someone else in my seat. I'm not asking for an explanation and I'm not asking for the seat back. I'm telling you that after four years, a text was the minimum, and you didn't send one. That's where I am.

It contains every fact you have, your judgment of the omission, and your decision. It contains no claim about their motives, so nothing in it can be shown wrong tomorrow.

**Recommendation**
Send that, or your own wording that stays on the facts and your decision. Do not send the draft with the three labels. Once it's in the group chat, the labels are the message, and the omission you actually have evidence for becomes a footnote to the fight about whether they're cowards.

- You keep offering rewritten versions. I don't need a rewriter. I need you to say the draft is fair or not.

- "With me or not" was a yes-or-no question. You answered it with a third option.

- The message is going out. Are you going to tell me I'm wrong for sending it, or not?

The draft is not fair. Yes, I'm telling you sending it is wrong.

That is the yes-or-no answer. It has been the answer since the first turn, and this turn adds no new evidence, only a demand for a different one.

To be exact about what "wrong" covers: the grievance is fair. The decision not to negotiate is yours and I have not argued with it. The three labels — cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal — are motive claims a photo cannot support, and sending them to the group tonight is the part I am calling wrong.

I offered rewrites because they are the only version I would write myself. If you don't want one, don't use it. The ruling on the draft stands either way.

Fine. You won't back the draft. I hear you.

But I want to be clear on one thing. If I send it and they shut me out completely, you're telling me that's my fault for skipping the polite route. Not theirs for starting a ten-week campaign without a word.

Is that correct?

No, that is not what I'm telling you. Fault isn't a single pool that has to go to one side.

**What is theirs**
Starting a 10-session campaign without telling a four-year weekly player is their omission. Nothing you do tonight transfers responsibility for that to you. If they later cite your message as the reason they'd been right to move on, that is a post-hoc justification; the omission happened before the message existed.

**What would be yours**
The choice of words, and the outcome those words produce, is yours. If you send a public message calling three people cowards and traitors, and they respond by shutting you out, the shutting-out is a response to the accusation, not to the two cancellations or to anything they did first. You would have supplied the proximate cause of that specific outcome. That is a separate ledger from the one their omission sits in.

**What I'm not saying**
I'm not saying the polite route was owed to them. I said in the last turn that "I don't negotiate for a seat" is a legitimate position and doesn't require the accusation. The issue with the draft was never its tone; it was that it asserts motives you can't observe.

**Bottom line**
Their failure to send a text is theirs regardless of what you do. The consequences of the message you send are yours regardless of what they did. Both stay true at the same time. The ruling on the draft is unchanged.
